claims.statement: Tom Allen and Mike McCoole quarrelled at Jack Looney's New Year's fancy ball, about 4 a.m. on January 2, 1873.
Tom Allen stayed at home taking longer walks to reduce to 170 pounds fighting weight, and would not go into training quarters for nearly two months.
Tom Allen said he was more afraid of his wife than of Mike McCoole, especially when he came home late at night.
A Democrat reporter asked Tom Allen whether he was afraid of the pugilist Mike McCoole.
Allen's emissaries claimed that when Allen called on McCoole last Sunday, McCoole kept out of his way; McCoole's trainer denied it.
Tom Allen was preparing for the McCoole fight and would then be ready for Charley Gallagher or any other man.
Tom Allen was reported to have done little training and to be reducing by walking before the McCoole fight.
Tom Allen was present at the fourth deposit at McCoole's saloon.
Arthur Chambers seconded Tom Allen in the fight with Mike McCoole.
Tom Allen did not appear at the final deposit.
Arthur Chambers and Patsey arrived in St. Louis from New York and were to second Tom Allen against McCoole.
Arthur Chambers and Palsy Shepherd seconded Tom Allen in his fight with McCoole.
Johnny Daly was Tom Allen's handler at the 1873 fight with Mike McCoole.
Arthur Chambers and Patsy Sheppard were expected to go into the ring as Tom Allen's seconds.
On the return trip Tom Allen started a subscription for Mike McCoole, headed it with $100, and the money was given to the trainers Madden and Tricks.
F. C. Cox won over $102 betting on Tom Allen on September 23, 1873.
Tom Allen received half of the $12,000 boat money from his second fight with Mike McCool.
Arthur Chambers and a second man named as 'Pater Ree' were Tom Allen's seconds and trainers for his fight with Mike McCoole.
Tom Allen said he planned to enjoy himself for two weeks and then return to training.
A bet of two hundred against one was placed in the hands of Joel Herbert a few evenings before the article (the paper's figures are garbled).
Arthur Chambers would again act as one of Tom Allen's seconds for the Hogan fight.
Mike McCoole was described as the opponent of Tom Allen.
John Looney suspected that Ben Hogan had arranged the failed excursion as a put-up job to avoid meeting Tom Allen.
Tom Allen has not yet begun training for the Hogan fight and will start only a few days before the contest.
Tom Allen will not begin training for the Hogan fight until about two weeks before it.
The odds favored Tom Allen over Ben Hogan, in some cases two to one.
Tom Allen was already in trim for the Hogan fight, while Ben Hogan was still getting in trim.
Arthur Chambers and Patsy Curtin were to second Tom Allen in the fight.
Arthur Chambers also seconded Tom Allen in the Hogan fight at East St. Louis.
Tom Allen denied fouling Ben Hogan, after Dr. C. E. Tennent had certified that Hogan was struck below the belt.
At the 1874 Springfield reunion, Tom Allen caught a pickpocket's hand and squeezed it, and the victim's outcry was the first alarm of a panic in the gallery.
Tom Allen was sitting in the second gallery with a friend when a pickpocket reached for his pocket at the 1874 Springfield reunion.
After the Allen-McCoole fight, the Missouri Legislature made prize-fighting a felony in January 1874.
Tom Allen said he sides with the legislature's bill against prize-fighting, because the ring has become corrupt.
Tom Allen said the bill had put his name in to mark him, and that the Times called him a refugee, which he denied.
Tom Allen was one of Edwards' seconds in Edwards' fight with Collyer near Pittsburg in August 1874.
About twenty years earlier Fred Watkins furnished something for Tom Allen (printed as 'Allen's apg').
Tom Allen appeared on the stage at the Comique benefit wearing his champion's belt and was greeted with loud applause.
At the audience's demand, Tom Allen sang three or four songs at the Comique benefit, although he was not on the bill as a singer.
Arthur Chambers, champion of the lightweights, put up $250 as a binder for Allen in the hands of Harry Gill for the Rooke match.
Tom Allen said he weighed 210 pounds (printed as '3i0') and had to train down before the Rooke fight.
The silver goblet presented to Tom Allen held a quart and cost $250.
Chamberlain declined to take part at the eleventh hour because some of his friends had money on Rooke and wanted their stakes back.
A report said Joe Coburn had organized a gang to go to Pittsburg and win the fight for Rooke by a staged foul if Rooke could not win.
Allen told the Republican the news of the new arrangements was new to him, and that Harry Hill was authorized to act for him.
Arthur Chambers and Billy Edwards attended to Allen's interests at the final deposit.
John Chamberlain was selected as final stakeholder for the Allen–Rooke match and accepted on June 1, 1875.
Shaughnessy, one of Rooke's backers, put an attachment on the stakes held by Harry Hill.
Jem Coyne of Newark wrote to Allen planning another match with Rooke and asked Allen to second him.
Harry Hill returned the $3,000 stakes from the first match and kept $1,000 of Allen's money to post for the new contest.
A rumour said Tom Allen was preparing for the stage and would make a debut in St. Louis in an American drama written for him.
Tom Allen was to appear on the stage in a sensational play written for him, playing a 'rough diamond' who rescues the heroine, under the supervision of a leading actress.
